texts.firmware.segaboot_gcm.about: The Triforce's own firmware. It is the program the arcade board starts from, and the cabinet's TEST switch opens a menu in it. The file is a 2 MiB image whose header reads RELSAB / SegaBoot. It is asked for only when 'Triforce: SegaBoot Firmware' is on.
texts.setting.anisotropy.about: Anisotropic texture filtering (Graphics > Enhancements). It makes textures seen at a flat angle sharper. 'default' leaves each texture as the game set it. It can change how the game runs and not only how it looks, because games read parts of their own picture back into the console's memory. A movie made with one value may not play back with another, so choose it when you create the project.
texts.setting.cpu_core.about: How the console's PowerPC processor is emulated. Each of the three choices gives the same result on every run and on every computer. They do NOT give the same result as each other. The cached interpreter and the JIT count time in blocks of instructions, and the interpreter counts every instruction, so the machine's timing differs and a movie made with one does not play back with another. 'jit' translates PowerPC code into your computer's own code and is the default because it is about five times faster. 'cached-interpreter' groups instructions into prepared blocks. 'interpreter' is the slowest and the most thoroughly tested.
texts.setting.gpu_texture_decoding.about: Decodes textures on the graphics card instead of the processor (Graphics > Hacks). It is meant to be faster. No difference in the picture or in the game was seen in the games tried here. Off is Dolphin's default.
texts.setting.internal_resolution.about: How many times the console's resolution the graphics card draws at (Graphics > Enhancements > Internal Resolution). Above 1x the picture Chimera shows and records is the sharper one the graphics card drew. For example a 640x448 game at 2x is 1280x896. It can change how the game runs and not only how it looks, because games read parts of their own picture back into the console's memory. A movie made with one value may not play back with another, so choose it when you create the project. Measured on Virtua Striker 2002, 2x changes the console's memory from the first 3D frame on, and the number of lag frames after 3000 fields is 547 against 585 at 1x. One limit: the sharper picture is not part of a savestate, so right after a state is loaded the picture can look different from a run that never stopped. The game itself is not affected, and a movie played from the start is sharp throughout.
texts.setting.lag_frames.about: Which frames are marked as lag frames, in red in TAStudio. 'picture' (No new picture, the default): a frame in which the game finished no new picture, that is, made no copy of its drawing to the buffer the screen shows. A game drawing 30 pictures a second shows every other frame as lag, and a loading screen that stops drawing shows lag throughout. 'controller' (Controller not read): a frame in which the console never read the first controller. A GameCube's serial chip reads the controllers by itself every frame once a game has started, so with this choice almost no frame is a lag frame. Neither choice changes the emulation; only the marks differ.
texts.setting.machine.about: Which machine this project is: a GameCube, a Wii, or a Triforce arcade board. The choice is saved in the project and recorded in the movie. The core never guesses it from the game file, and a game for another machine is refused. A GameCube has memory card slots, and a Wii keeps its saves in its internal memory (NAND). 'triforce' is the arcade board that Sega, Namco and Nintendo built from GameCube hardware (Virtua Striker, F-Zero AX, Mario Kart Arcade GP). A Triforce disc image is marked as such, and the project must say 'triforce' to start one.
texts.setting.memcard_a.about: Whether a memory card is in the first slot. Games check for a card on their first screen and behave differently without one, so this is part of the machine. The card's contents are not chosen here. They come from the project's save data and go back to it.
texts.setting.mmu.about: Dolphin's full memory-management emulation (Config > Advanced > Enable MMU). A few games need it to run correctly, and TASVideos requires it for those. Off is Dolphin's default. On is slower. It changes how the processor behaves, with either renderer, so a movie records it and needs the same value to play back.
texts.setting.msaa.about: Multisample anti-aliasing (Graphics > Enhancements > Anti-Aliasing). It smooths the edges of what the graphics card draws. It can change how the game runs and not only how it looks, because games read parts of their own picture back into the console's memory. A movie made with one value may not play back with another, so choose it when you create the project.
texts.setting.port1.about: What is plugged into controller port 1. With the port empty, games find nothing connected there, as on a real console, and some games behave differently. The port's buttons and sticks are then also removed from the input columns and from the movie. On a Wii the port can instead hold Wii Remote 1: "wii-remote" alone, "wii-remote-nunchuk" with a Nunchuk, or "classic-controller" with a Classic Controller (whose buttons are then the port's, and the Wii Remote's own are not used). A Wii Remote has its buttons, a pointer (Pointer X and Y, where it points on the screen, which the mouse drives out of the box), Shake (a shake every way at once) and Tilt X and Y; it has no free motion and no MotionPlus. A GameCube project refuses a Wii controller.

texts.setting.renderer.about: Which renderer draws the picture. 'software' is Dolphin's software renderer. It runs completely inside the sandbox and gives the same picture on every computer, so choose it when a movie must play back on computers different from yours. 'opengl-hw' is Dolphin's OpenGL renderer drawing on your REAL graphics card through the bridge. It is much faster and looks best. The graphics card is outside the sandbox and differs between computers, and parts of the picture are copied back into the console's memory, so a movie recorded this way plays back only on the same graphics driver. On a computer with no usable graphics card the core draws in software and says so. 'vulkan-hw' is Dolphin's Vulkan renderer drawing on your graphics card. What is said of 'opengl-hw' is true of it, and a movie recorded with one of the two may not play back with the other. It has nothing to fall back on: it needs a graphics driver that has Vulkan and a Chimera that hands Vulkan to cores, and without either the project does not start and says why.
texts.setting.ssaa.about: Turns the anti-aliasing above into supersampling, which also smooths the inside of textures and effects and costs more graphics time. It does nothing while Anti-Aliasing is off. It can change how the game runs and not only how it looks, because games read parts of their own picture back into the console's memory. A movie made with one value may not play back with another, so choose it when you create the project.
texts.setting.texture_cache.about: How carefully Dolphin checks whether a texture in the game's memory has changed (Graphics > Hacks > Texture Cache Accuracy). 'safe' checks the whole texture and notices games that change one in place. 'fast' is Dolphin's default. No difference was seen in the games tried here (up to 3000 fields, including 3D scenes). Where a game does change textures in place, 'safe' draws it correctly and the others may not. It can change how the game runs and not only how it looks, because games read parts of their own picture back into the console's memory. A movie made with one value may not play back with another, so choose it when you create the project.
texts.setting.texture_filtering.about: Forces every texture to be drawn either blocky (nearest) or smoothed (linear) (Graphics > Enhancements > Texture Filtering). 'default' leaves each texture as the game set it. It can change how the game runs and not only how it looks, because games read parts of their own picture back into the console's memory. A movie made with one value may not play back with another, so choose it when you create the project.
texts.setting.triforce_segaboot.about: Gives the arcade cabinet its own firmware, SegaBoot. The cabinet's TEST switch opens a menu in this firmware, and without it the switch does nothing. Most games never need it. Mario Kart Arcade GP is the exception. It stops at CAMERA ERROR because there is no camera here, and the camera is turned off in the test menu. The firmware is a file you supply (segaboot.gcm, 2 MiB). Whether the cabinet has it is part of the machine, so a movie needs the same choice.
texts.setting.widescreen.about: The Wii's own system setting 'Screen: Widescreen'. A Wii game reads it to decide whether to draw for a 16:9 or a 4:3 screen, and many games draw differently for each, so it is part of the machine and a movie records it. Off means 4:3, which is what a new console is set to. The picture Chimera shows stays 640 pixels wide in both cases. To see a widescreen game in its intended shape, set Config > Display > Aspect Ratio Selection > 'Use custom AR' to 16:9.
texts.setting.widescreen_hack.about: Dolphin's widescreen hack (Graphics > General). The game's 3D view is widened to fill a 16:9 screen. The picture keeps the console's own width, so it looks squeezed until you set Config > Display > Aspect Ratio to 16:9. The 2D parts of a game (menus, status displays) are not widened and may look stretched. It can change how the game runs and not only how it looks, because games read parts of their own picture back into the console's memory. A movie made with one value may not play back with another, so choose it when you create the project.
texts.slot.game.help: The game. It can be a disc image (.iso or .gcm, or Dolphin's .rvz), a homebrew program (.dol or .elf) that is started directly, or a Wii channel (.wad, as used for WiiWare and Virtual Console games). A .wad makes this a Wii project. It is installed into the console's internal memory before the machine starts and launched from there, as the Wii Menu would do. A game on several discs takes every disc image, in order: the first is in the drive when the console is switched on, and the Next Disc, Previous Disc and Disc Swap controls change it when the game asks.
texts.slot.savedata.help: The saved data the machine starts with. Put back exactly what Emulator > Export Save Data... wrote, to continue a run from where another one stopped. The file is never changed, and the project and the movie record exactly which file it was. For a GameCube it is the memory card image under the same name (MemoryCardA.USA.raw, or .EUR. or .JAP. according to the game's region). Leave it empty and the machine starts with an empty, formatted card. For a Wii it is the .zip that Export Save Data writes, holding the game's own save files from the console's internal memory (nand/title/.../data/...). They are put into the game's save folder before it starts. A save from a different game is refused.
